name: Barna Group research on AI in churches and faith organisations
title: Barna Group research on AI in churches and faith organisations
answer: Barna Group's AI research pages report U.S. survey data on how adults, Christians and pastors perceive and use artificial intelligence, produced with Gloo for the State of the Church initiative. The most useful finding for church leaders is the gap between caution and practical openness: 94 percent of pastors are concerned about AI misinterpreting scripture, yet 77 percent agree God can work through AI, 88 percent are comfortable with AI assisting graphic design and only 12 percent are comfortable with AI writing sermons. The pages quantify adoption, generational differences and pastoral comfort.

sections.body: Barna Group publishes these research articles on barna.com. They come from its AI and the Church study and Faith & AI project, conducted in partnership with Gloo and tied to the State of the Church initiative. The pages report surveys of U.S. adults, practicing Christians, pastors, parents and generational groups on AI perception, personal and workplace use, pastoral comfort, relationships and scripture interpretation. One article states a survey of 1,067 U.S. adults conducted May 21 to 31, 2024, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.0 percent at the 95 percent confidence level. Other pages read do not state dates.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Across the pages, Barna reports that U.S. adults hold mixed views of AI. One in three adults, 32 percent, find AI exciting, 33 percent find it scary and 41 percent call it concerning. Christians are similar, at 30 percent exciting and 34 percent scary, but pastors are far more cautious: 72 percent call AI concerning and only 9 percent see it as encouraging. Usage varies. Barna says 31 percent of U.S. adults use AI weekly or daily, rising to 43 percent of Millennials, while 68 percent feel no urgency to integrate AI into their lives. In work, 34 percent of working adults use AI often or sometimes, and 39 percent of working Christians do so at least sometimes compared with 26 percent of working non-Christians. Adults are most interested in AI for answering questions, 37 percent, and research, 35 percent, and least interested in advice, 14 percent, or spiritual questions, 8 percent. Pastors are open to administrative uses: 88 percent are comfortable with AI assisting graphic design, 78 percent with marketing, 58 percent with communication, 43 percent with sermon preparation and research, but only 12 percent with writing sermons and 6 percent with counseling. Barna also reports that 94 percent of pastors are concerned about AI misinterpreting scripture, and 60 percent say AI should present all major interpretations without naming one correct.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: Barna gives several definitions and benchmarks. It defines AI as technology that makes machines capable of tasks that typically require human intelligence, including understanding language, recognizing patterns and making decisions. In its explanation experiment, concern about AI fell from 51 percent to 42 percent after respondents read that definition. Barna reports that 45 percent of U.S. adults regularly use smart home devices, 42 percent use in-device assistants such as Siri and 40 percent use facial recognition, all of which it says utilize AI. On generational trust, 45 percent of Boomers say they do not trust AI, compared with 18 percent of Gen Z, 21 percent of Millennials and 25 percent of Gen X, and 18 percent of Boomers trust AI to be objective and accurate, compared with 49 percent of Gen Z and 50 percent of Millennials. On relationships, 89 percent of pastors expect AI to affect relational quality, 56 percent of those negatively, and 74 percent agree a person could develop an emotional connection to AI while 65 percent agree a person could develop a romantic connection. On scripture, 74 percent of U.S. adults, 83 percent of practicing Christians and 94 percent of pastors are concerned about AI misinterpreting scripture. Barna also reports that 77 percent of pastors agree God can work through AI, 95 percent are concerned about privacy and data security, and 78 percent agree AI could worsen current social inequalities.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone following AI in churches and faith organisations, these pages supply rare quantitative evidence about the people in the pews and the pulpit. They show that pastors are not simply rejecting AI: most see potential for God to work through it and are comfortable with administrative and creative uses, while drawing sharp lines at sermons, counseling and scripture interpretation. They also show a communication gap, since only 11 percent of Christians see their pastors as someone to help them learn about AI, and just 13 percent want to hear from their pastor on a theology of AI usage or on using AI to grow in faith. The data can inform adoption policies, preaching, training and tool choices.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Churches and Faith Organisations

sections.body: The pages are separate research articles rather than one comprehensive report, and several are produced in partnership with Gloo, so readers should note the partnership. The data are U.S. focused and do not provide denominational breakdowns, non-U.S. comparisons or evaluations of specific AI products. One article dates its survey to May 2024, while other pages read do not state dates. The research measures perceptions and self-reported use, not measured outcomes or theological conclusions.
